title: Torsion orders in Fowler's arithmetic FH(ℚ) lattices
question: Fowler's Section 5 constructs arithmetic lattices in semisimple groups and shows they lie in FH(\mathbb Q). Which torsion orders can actually occur in these examples, and how do the number-theoretic choices (quadratic fields, quaternion algebras, etc.) control the finite subgroups that appear in the resulting lattices?
answer: Start with an absolutely almost simple \mathbb Q-group \mathbf G that is anisotropic over \mathbb Q at infinity (for instance, the norm-one group of a quaternion algebra that ramifies at every real place). Let F/\mathbb Q be a number field and choose an order \mathcal O\subset F. The arithmetic lattice \Gamma=\mathbf G(\mathcal O) embeds cocompactly in the real Lie group G=\mathbf G(\mathbb R). Finite subgroups of \Gamma are precisely the torsion units of \mathbf G(\mathcal O), so their orders divide the orders of elements in \mathbf G(\mathcal O_F), where F is the splitting field of \mathbf G.\n\nFor quaternion-algebra examples the torsion comes from the roots of unity in F. Choosing F=\mathbb Q(i) or \mathbb Q(\zeta_3) produces lattices with 4- or 6-torsion; taking F with class number one and no nontrivial roots of unity yields torsion-free lattices. Thus Fowler's arithmetic constructions realize every torsion order that already occurs among the units of the chosen number field. Each such lattice still lies in FH(\mathbb Q) because the associated orbicomplex satisfies the fixed-set Euler-vanishing hypothesis, but only the torsion-free specializations give genuine manifold quotients.
